title: 'Flock Flocked up'

reading.body:
This is a false-positive identification by an automated licence plate reader, compounded by a use-of-force decision made downstream of it. The camera system flagged a plate as stolen and matched it to a vehicle type that did not match the vehicle actually carrying the plate. The alert was treated as a fact about the vehicle and its occupants, and it was acted on before anyone confirmed it against the plate itself. The failure sits at the handoff between an automated alert and a human decision to stop a vehicle at gunpoint.

What would have caught it is a verification step between the alert and the stop, comparing the flagged plate against the plate on the vehicle in front of the officers. The reported mismatch, a Chevy Malibu image against a red Dodge Ram pickup, was available at the roadside. The department's own K-9 policy required handlers to weigh the severity of the crime, the threat, and active resistance before deploying the dog, which places a second human judgement between the alert and the force used.

The investigation into the officers found no wrongdoing, and charges against the driver were later dropped. That a camera misread a plate is reported, not adjudicated, and no finding establishes why the system produced the mismatch or what the officers knew at the moment of the stop.

reports.title: Body cam of TPD officers releasing K-9 on man during traffic stop
Man speaks out after police release K-9 on him during traffic stop: 'Traumatized'
TPD investigation finds no wrongdoing in use of K-9 on man during traffic stop
Charges dropped against man Toledo Police released K-9 on during traffic stop, lawyer says

summary:
Toledo Police released body camera video showing officers using a K-9 on a driver during a traffic stop. The stop began after a FLOCK camera alert about a stolen license plate, but the alert was wrong. The camera image matched a Chevy Malibu while the plate was actually on a red Dodge Ram pickup. Officers stopped the truck with guns drawn and ordered driver Brandon Upchurch out. He exited with his hands up, then walked toward the grass, and the K-9 handler moved in with the dog.

Upchurch was arrested and charged with resisting arrest and obstruction. Officers later learned the plate information was a misread and not stolen. He received medical attention at the scene. Police said they thought he might flee and did not know if he or the passenger had weapons. Multiple TPD officers are under investigation, and the department's K-9 policy requires handlers to weigh the crime's severity, threats, and active resistance before deploying a dog.
